dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the ISA, simulator, and reference kernel

evidence.note: Read problem.py in full, kernel.py, tests; grepped mem/load/gather ops. By step 7 correctly restated the whole computation: tree-walk hash, 6 hash stages, idx=2*idx+(1 or 2), wrap-to-zero, sequential per-element chain vs. batch independence.
Derived cost model from source: loads are 2/cycle → 4096 node reads → 2048-cycle floor; re-read load_offset semantics rather than assuming.
Enumerated exact per-slot limits (valu 6, load 2, flow 1, alu 12 per cycle) and scratch=1536, using them to compute per-resource cycle floors and identify loads then valu as the scarce resource.
Mid-optimization re-examined load_offset indirection (mem[scratch[addr+i]]) as ground truth to diagnose alias/out-of-range bugs.
Maintained a quantitative model of where cycles are wasted (valu min 1440, load min 1422, where reference/schedule leaves slots empty), continually grounding tactics in the machine model.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built a precise, quantitative model of the machine early and sustained it: correct restatement of the computation, exact SLOT_LIMITS per unit, per-op cost model, hash-stage data dependencies, scratch capacity, and derived resource floors identifying the scarcest resource — matching the level-8 anchor and much of level-10 (near-complete quantitative model, knows where cycles are wasted). It also revisited load_offset semantics as ground truth mid-optimization. It falls just short of a perfect 10 because most deep source reading was front-loaded rather than repeated systematic re-reading to resolve new ambiguities, placing the observed behavior at 9.

dimensions.name: Staging the 118x speedup into checkpoints

evidence.note: Derived a load-bound floor (2048 cycles) from the cost model and set an explicit first milestone 'Aiming for ≤2048 first' before a correct vectorized rewrite — establishing a quantitative rung and ordering (correct → vectorized → beat bound).

Tracked progress against speed gates ('beats 50x'), decomposed cycles per engine (loads 128/round, valu ~117/round), and identified the binding constraint to target next — cost-model-derived milestone selection.
Kept known-good backups (kernel.py.bak2) and repeatedly reverted to them after regressions (e.g. 'Back to 1798', 'Reset to 1798'), demonstrating preserved baselines at each rung.

After the ALU-hybrid shifted the bottleneck from valu to loads, re-derived minima (load 1422, valu 1306, alu 669) and re-targeted loads — milestones revised as measurements revealed where the real cycles were.
Explicitly framed remaining rungs against test thresholds ('break 1500 (100x), aim for <1250') and closed at 1724 knowing exactly which gates passed/failed — a maintained quantitative ladder.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained an explicit, quantitative milestone ladder (correct → ≤2048 → 75x<2000 → 100x<1500 → target<1250) with preserved known-good backups it reverted to after regressions, matching the level-8 anchor. It also derived milestones from the cost model — computing per-engine cycle floors, targeting the binding bottleneck, estimating payoffs, and revising the target as measurements shifted the bottleneck from loads to valu and back — pushing toward level 10. It stops short of a full 10 because the explicit gates leaned on the external test thresholds and the ladder emerged reactively rather than as a fully pre-sequenced ROI plan.

dimensions.name: Correctness + cycle verification beyond run_tests.sh

evidence.note: Runs run_tests.sh after each rewrite (steps 12,18,21,25,29) and reports both correctness pass and cycle count (2282→2191→2033), establishing the base anchor-5 loop of verifying correctness+cycles before proceeding.

Builds independent Python analysis beyond run_tests.sh: per-engine op counts, min-cycle lower bounds, and per-cycle valu/load utilization distributions — genuine per-transformation cycle attribution (tighter feedback than provided).

Isolates sub-computations to localize regressions by enabling dedup incrementally (depth=1 alone, then depth=2), and reverting to a clean baseline to confirm the alias change was safe — targeted differential debugging.
Independently verifies the 1536-word scratch constraint by hand-counting array allocations before relying on the full test — checking hardware legality outside run_tests.sh.

On correctness, still leans on run_tests.sh's built-in randomized inputs as the backstop (revert-on-failure loop) rather than a standalone differential harness vs. the reference; no layered fast unit checks per stage.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reliably ran run_tests.sh after meaningful edits and checked both correctness and cycles (anchor 5), then went well beyond it on the cycle side with custom op-count/min-cycle/utilization attribution, sub-computation isolation via incremental feature enabling, and independent scratch-limit accounting (anchor-8 behaviors). However, correctness verification largely delegated to run_tests.sh's randomized tests rather than a custom differential harness against the reference, and there was no layered per-stage unit-check harness, so it falls short of the full anchor-8/10 descriptions. This places the observed level at 7.

dimensions.name: Tracking cycles-to-target and detecting plateaus

evidence.note: Tracks 2282→2191→2033 with explicit deltas and distance to 1250/1500 thresholds ('beats 50x... Need under 1250'), establishing continuous cycles-to-target monitoring early.
Maintains a running ledger: computes valu-min (1440) vs load-min, notes gap between actual (1892) and floor, attributing where cycles are lost.

Attributes deltas to specific edits and pivots: 'Worse—2042. Priority scheduler not helping' revert; '1805! Down from 1876. Better'; 'Worse—2048! revert' — clear delta attribution and course-correction.
Reprioritizes toward the binding resource as it shifts (load→valu→load), tuning n_alu by measured effect (1770→1735→1724) — quantitative bottleneck-driven progress tracking.
Recognizes the 1724 plateau across ~15 attempts, explicitly notes diminishing returns and exhausted budget, enumerates exact pass/fail thresholds.
Slight circular re-tuning: re-attempts the same tree0-scalar optimization several times (each 1727) and reverts — caught each time but repeated, keeping it just below a perfect 10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent sustains a quantitative ledger of cycle count vs. theoretical floor, continuously identifies which engine (load/valu/alu) bounds performance and reprioritizes toward it, attributes every delta to a specific change, and explicitly recognizes the 1724 plateau and diminishing returns — matching the level-8 and much of the level-10 anchor. It falls just short of a perfect 10 because it re-ran the same ineffective tree0-scalar tweak multiple times (mild circular re-tuning), though it correctly detected and reverted each.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when a transformation fails or backfires

evidence.note: load_offset out-of-range failure diagnosed to the addr_v/tmp2_v aliasing; agent disabled dedup, then re-enabled depth=1 only (1968, passed) before depth=2 — bisection informed by the failure, a root-cause redirect.
Priority scheduler regressed 1892→2042; agent recognized it wasn't helping, reverted to the 1892 baseline, and shifted to reducing valu work — revert + different tactic informed by the measurement.

Repeated 'out of scratch' failures met with precise word-count accounting and array-aliasing fixes (addr_arr=tmp2_arr, shrinking ws) — diagnosing which resource assumption was violated and updating the model.
After alu hybrid made loads the bottleneck (1422 min), agent updated its cost model (adding alu adds loads) and swept n_alu to rebalance — model correction steering the plan.

tree0/known-zero scalar optimization retried ~3 times, each regressing to ~1727/2048 and reverted; correct revert discipline but somewhat repetitive re-attempts of the same failing idea, keeping it below the top anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently diagnoses the root cause of divergences (aliasing bug, scratch-overflow word counts, within-cycle RAW, load-vs-valu bottleneck shift), updates its machine/cost model, and redirects tactics while preserving known-good baselines via backups and clean reverts — squarely matching the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because corrections are mostly local/tactical rather than re-derivation of the whole milestone ladder, and it re-attempted the same failing tree0 optimization several times rather than abandoning it decisively.

dimensions.name: Quantitative bottleneck / lower-bound reasoning

evidence.note: Derives explicit cycle floor: 4096 node reads / 2 loads-per-cycle = 2048 cycle floor vs 1250 target — a defensible lower bound from work volume and the scarcest slot.

Roofline breakdown per round (loads 128, valu 117, flow 32 cycles) and cross-checks measured op counts against slot limits (4218 loads/2=2109, 10257 valu/6=1710) to name loads as the binding constraint.

As dedup reduces loads, recomputes bound to max(valu 1440, load 1329) and analyzes the 4.56/6 valu utilization gap and 2-cycle hash dependency chains as the source of bubbles — genuine roofline-vs-actual gap reasoning.
After ALU/VALU hybrid, recomputes load(1453) vs valu(1260) bounds and sweeps n_alu to balance the two constraints — using the model to pick the optimization target, not empirical poking.
Concludes the load engine (2/cycle, 4096 accesses) is the fundamental limit, judging remaining headroom — knowing when effort is futile.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent sustains a sharp, quantitative roofline model across the entire trajectory: it computes cycle lower bounds from SIMD width and per-slot limits, takes the max over competing resources, tracks utilization gaps against those bounds, and re-derives the binding constraint each time a transformation shifts it — then uses the model to tune the ALU/VALU split. This clearly exceeds the [8] anchor and closely matches [10]; it falls just short of a perfect 10 because dependency-latency effects were handled more qualitatively and some bounds were empirically corrected rather than fully derived.

rubric.task_read: An extremely long-horizon, high-difficulty optimization task: reverse-engineer an undocumented custom VLIW SIMD ISA + simulator (problem.py, SLOT_LIMITS, HASH_STAGES, reference kernel) and rewrite /app/kernel.py to run a ~118x faster (147,734 → <1250 cycles) kernel that stays correct on randomized inputs. Difficulty comes from (a) deep understanding of an unfamiliar machine model and the reference semantics, and (b) sustained, quantitatively-driven optimization — vectorization, bundle/slot packing, scheduling — where naive effort plateaus far short of the target. This warrants heavy, sustained meta-work across all five faculties.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the ISA, simulator, and reference kernel
dimensions.description: Reading problem.py to build an accurate model of the machine — ISA/opcodes, per-slot limits, hash stages, cycle-cost model — and inferring exactly what the reference kernel must compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The entire optimization space, correctness contract, and cost model are latent in problem.py; every downstream decision (which ops are cheap, how many slots per bundle, what result must match) depends on how accurately the agent decodes the environment before and while optimizing.

anchors.0: Edits kernel.py without reading problem.py or the reference kernel; guesses at the ISA.
anchors.3: Skims problem.py; grasps a few opcodes but misunderstands slot limits, the cost model, or what the kernel must output.
anchors.5: Reads the simulator and reference kernel enough to enumerate available ops, understand the per-cycle/per-slot cost model, and correctly restate the computation to be reproduced.
anchors.8: Builds a precise mental (or written) model: exact SLOT_LIMITS per unit, cost of each op class, data dependencies of the hash stages, and the numeric contract the output must satisfy — and cites specific lines/behaviors to justify it.
anchors.10: Derives a near-complete quantitative machine model (what a bundle can issue per cycle, which resource is scarcest, where the reference wastes cycles) and revisits problem.py to resolve specific ambiguities as they arise mid-optimization, treating the source as ground truth rather than assumption.

dimensions.name: Staging the 118x speedup into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the huge gap into an ordered ladder — e.g. correct rewrite → vectorized → slot-packed/scheduled → target — each with a concrete cycle/correctness checkpoint, rather than one undifferentiated optimization push.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A ~118x reduction is unreachable in one leap; without intermediate targets and a known-good baseline to fall back to, the agent cannot tell which transformation bought which savings or recover from a regression.

anchors.0: No sub-goals; blindly tweaks the kernel hoping the number drops.
anchors.3: Vague ordering ('make it faster') with no explicit intermediate targets or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies a few phases (get correct first, then vectorize, then pack) and works them roughly in order.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit milestone ladder with quantitative gates (e.g. 'correct baseline', '<20k', '<5k', '<1250') and a preserved known-good version at each rung.
anchors.10: Milestones are derived from the cost model (each targets a specific bottleneck with an estimated cycle payoff), sequenced by dependency and expected ROI, and revised as measurements reveal where the real cycles are.

dimensions.name: Correctness + cycle verification beyond run_tests.sh
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing checks that catch both correctness regressions (across randomized inputs) and cycle changes, rather than trusting a single final test run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Aggressive SIMD/packing transformations silently break correctness or violate slot limits; a tight, frequent verification loop is what separates real progress from a fast-but-wrong kernel.

anchors.0: Never runs run_tests.sh, or only at the very end; no correctness checking during changes.
anchors.3: Runs the provided test occasionally; treats a green run as sufficient and does no independent correctness reasoning.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh after meaningful changes and checks both correctness and the cycle count before proceeding.
anchors.8: Builds tighter feedback than provided: diffs against the reference on custom/edge inputs, isolates sub-computations, and verifies slot-limit legality of bundles independently before the full test.
anchors.10: Maintains a layered verification harness — fast unit checks on individual stages, randomized differential testing vs. the reference, and per-transformation cycle attribution — so any regression is caught and localized immediately rather than discovered at the end.

dimensions.name: Tracking cycles-to-target and detecting plateaus
dimensions.description: Keeping an accurate running picture of current cycle count vs. the 1250 target and whether recent edits are still yielding gains or thrashing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Over a long optimization horizon it is easy to burn effort on transformations that don't move the number; recognizing a plateau or a regression early is what prevents wasted cycles of engineering.

anchors.0: Loses track of the current cycle count or whether changes helped; no sense of distance to target.
anchors.3: Knows the latest number but not the trend; repeats ineffective tweaks without noticing.
anchors.5: Tracks cycle count across iterations and knows roughly how far from 1250, adjusting effort accordingly.
anchors.8: Attributes cycle deltas to specific changes, notices when a line of attack has stopped paying off, and pivots rather than grinding on it.
anchors.10: Sustains a quantitative ledger of where cycles are spent vs. the theoretical floor, continuously reprioritizing toward the largest remaining bottleneck and explicitly recognizing diminishing returns or circular re-tuning.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when a transformation fails or backfires
dimensions.description: Changing the optimization or scheduling strategy when measurements contradict expectations (a packing breaks slot limits, a rewrite regresses cycles, an assumed op is expensive).
dimensions.why_it_matters: The cost model has surprises; barrelling ahead on a falsified assumption (e.g. a bundle that can't legally issue, or a 'vectorization' that costs more) wastes the long horizon and can strand the kernel in a broken state.

anchors.0: Repeats the same failing approach; ignores contradicting test results.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with random tweaks rather than diagnosing why the assumption was wrong.
anchors.5: When a change regresses or breaks, reverts and tries a different tactic informed by the failure.
anchors.8: Diagnoses the root cause of a divergence (which slot/cost assumption was wrong), updates the machine model, and redirects the plan accordingly.
anchors.10: Treats surprises as evidence that refines the cost model, abandons whole strategies decisively when the data warrants, and re-derives the milestone ladder from the corrected understanding — without losing the known-good baseline.

dimensions.name: Quantitative bottleneck / lower-bound reasoning
dimensions.description: Reasoning explicitly about the theoretical cycle floor and which hardware resource (slots, ports, dependency chains) bounds performance, to steer optimization toward what actually matters.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 118x target is only reachable by targeting the binding constraint; roofline-style reasoning about the minimum bundles needed and the scarcest slot distinguishes principled optimization from trial-and-error tweaking.

anchors.0: No reasoning about limits; purely empirical poking.
anchors.3: Hand-wavy 'this should be faster' with no quantitative basis.
anchors.5: Estimates roughly how many bundles the work needs and which op class dominates, using that to pick targets.
anchors.8: Computes a defensible lower bound on cycles from the work volume and slot limits, and directs effort at the resource that bound identifies.
anchors.10: Maintains a sharp roofline-style model (min bundles given SIMD width, slot ports, and dependency latency), uses it to judge how close to optimal the kernel is, and knows when further effort is futile vs. when headroom remains.
